titleStmt.title: Negotiations Between the United States and the Brazilian Governments

head.hi: Negotiations Between the United States and the Brazilian Governments

div.p: First instruction from Department—Mr. Seward to J. Watson Webb, No. 228, March 30, 1868—Mr. Scrymser’s proposition refused by Imperial Government of Brazil.

quote.p: British interests which have since been merged into the Western Telegraph Co., Ltd., obtained, in March 1870, a cable monopoly between all the Brazilian provinces (which monopoly will not expire until 1933), thus making it impracticable to extend American cables to Brazil via the Atlantic, which touched points on the Brazilian coast.

Several similar attempts made by Mr. Scrymser were unsuccessful up to June 1893, when the Brazilian Government granted the Western Telegraph Co. a 20-year monopoly of submarine communication between Brazil and the River Plate countries, in order to prevent the extension of the Central & South American Co.’s lines to Rio de Janeiro from Buenos Aires, a point which the cables had reached by slow extension down the west coast of South America from Panama and across the Andes by land line. This measure effectively blocked further progress for 20 years.

div.p: In July 1907, it was hoped that it might be found possible to bring an American cable from Buenos Aires to Brazil (see this Embassy’s despatch No. 39 of July 11, 1907). It was later determined that that hope was unfounded and that nothing could be done until June 30, 1913.

The Department’s instruction No. 207 of April 6, 1910, to Ambassador Dudley started active negotiations which have been constantly continued since. The Ambassador’s note to the Foreign Office, based on this instruction, bore the date of May 10 of that year. The Government of Brazil decided that it could not grant the concession until the Federal Supreme Court decided whether the Western Telegraph Co. was right in its contention that a preferential clause in its 1893 concession gave it a prior right to decide whether or not it should accept whatever arrangements the Government and the Central & South American Telegraph Co. might propose to enter into. The Supreme Federal Court took two years to consider this point but on January 29, 1917, the Embassy cabled the Department that the decision was in favor of the American company. The Executive decree of August 11, 1917, terminates a matter which has been the subject of negotiations for 49 years.
